messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
EHR Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Undisclosed
Age: 31 
Admission Date: Undisclosed 
Discharge Date: Undisclosed 

Hospital Course Summary:
Admission Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course: The patient was initially treated with oral mesalamine and prednisolone but in 2010 was changed to azathioprine. The disease continued to relapse despite azathioprine therapy. In 2014, adalimumab was initiated after screening for infectious diseases. The patient was found positive for the presence of mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB) by the QuantiFERON®-TB Gold test (QFT-G). INH preventive therapy was started and 14 weeks later the patient developed erythematous plaques on the neck and back with clear zones of demarcation resembling sunburn erythema on the dorsum of his hands, and hyperkeratotic plaques on the elbows. The patient reported frequent diarrheal stools, loss of appetite, and episodes of delirium and behavioral changes. Pellagra was suspected due to the low serum niacin level. Pharmacovigilance survey confirmed INH-induced pellagra. The management plan included INH withdrawal, nutritional review, and vitamin supplementation. The patient was treated with niacin orally (200mg/d). Three weeks later, the rash disappeared and diarrhea stopped. The patient was subsequently started on adalimumab.
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Condition on Discharge: The patient’s clinical symptoms improved after treatment with niacin and adalimumab. No rash or diarrhea was reported.

Discharge Medications: None

Follow-Up: Follow-up with the gastroenterology team is recommended to ensure the patient's Crohn's disease is managed appropriately. No follow-up for the management of INH-induced pellagra is necessary.

Instructions: The patient is advised to maintain a healthy diet and avoid foods that may cause vitamin B3 deficiency. No further precautions are required.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The admission was for pellagra, a niacin deficiency caused by isoniazid (INH) preventive therapy, presenting with rash, diarrhoea and delirium. Pellagra is a nutritional deficiency, so it falls under chapter E, and niacin deficiency is category E52. Crohn's disease was the underlying comorbidity, not the reason for this admission.

CODE: E52
